analysis.one_liner: Caps how many patents brand biologic makers can use to sue cheaper biosimilar competitors.
analysis.headline: Cleared a House committee by voice vote in September 2021 but never received a House floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company tries to sell a cheaper copy of an expensive biologic drug, the brand-name maker can sue it for patent infringement — sometimes using dozens of patents. This bill would limit the brand maker to asserting 20 patents in such a lawsuit, with courts able to raise the number when justice requires. Fewer patents to fight means less litigation expense and delay, so cheaper biosimilars would reach the market sooner. The bill cleared committee but never got a vote on the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take expensive biologic drugs — such as treatments for arthritis, cancer, and diabetes — because faster biosimilar competition tends to push prices down. Biosimilar manufacturers also gain by facing a more predictable, smaller set of lawsuits.

how_it_helps.text: Limits the reference product sponsor to asserting no more than 20 patents, of which no more than 10 may be late-filed patents issued more than four years after approval, in a lawsuit against a biosimilar applicant that completes the required information-sharing steps [S3].

The CRS summary states the bill limits the number of patents a biologic maker can assert against a company seeking to sell a biosimilar in lawsuits filed under the abbreviated FDA approval pathway [S2].
Applies to biosimilar applications submitted on or after enactment, so new biosimilars would enter a litigation process with fewer patents to litigate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic manufacturers, which would lose part of the patent-thicket litigation strategy that has kept biosimilar copies off the market and kept their drug prices high. Patients would bear no direct cost; any easing of litigation risks slightly less revenue for brands whose patents would no longer all be assertable.

drawbacks.text: The cap is generous: a brand maker could still assert up to 20 patents per suit, and the bill expressly exempts patents claiming a method of using the drug in therapy or diagnosis from the limit — a category of patents often used in thicket litigation [S3].

Courts can raise the number of assertable patents for good cause, including when the biosimilar applicant fails to share required information or when the product changes materially, giving brand makers a path around the cap [S3].

The limit applies only if the biosimilar applicant completes all the required steps of the negotiation process with the brand maker, so a biosimilar company that does not engage loses the protection [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a real but partial fix. Cutting the number of patents a brand maker can litigate would lower legal costs and delay for biosimilar entrants, which over time lowers prices for patients. But the 20-patent ceiling, the method-of-use carve-out, and the court's good-cause escape valve leave brand makers considerable room to keep litigating, so the price relief would be gradual rather than dramatic. Still, the main reason patients got no benefit from this bill is that it never came to a floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it by voice vote in September 2021, but no one ever scheduled it for a vote by the full House before that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Introduced April 28, 2021 by Rep. Hank Johnson with Rep. Darrell Issa, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1][S3][S5].
The committee held a markup on September 30, 2021 and ordered the bill reported in the nature of a substitute by voice vote [S5].
After being ordered reported, the bill received no further action — no committee report, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic manufacturers keep the full patent-thicket litigation strategy the bill would have trimmed, and biosimilar competition continues to arrive later and after more lawsuits than the bill would have allowed.

for.name: Rep. Hank C. 'Hank' Johnson, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and saw it through a committee markup that ordered it reported by voice vote.

for.name: Rep. Darrell Issa
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its Republican cosponsor.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: Controlled the House floor calendar in the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote after it cleared committee, and it expired at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and a Republican cosponsor from introduction, and the committee ordered it reported by voice vote, with no recorded party split at any stage [S3][S4][S5].

industries.note: Biologic makers defend their high prices partly by amassing dozens of patents and suing each biosimilar entrant over each one, a practice the bill would cap at 20 patents with court exceptions. Each year of delayed biosimilar entry is continued monopoly pricing that patients pay for [S2][S3].

Biosimilar companies would face a smaller, more predictable set of infringement claims, cutting the legal cost and delay that keep cheaper versions off the market. Their gain (reaching market sooner) runs alongside patients' gain of lower prices [S2][S3].
